criterion_notes.c1: Examines household and settlement-level access to drinking water and sewerage networks, dry fire-hydrant networks, rainwater collectors, and municipal water tanker delivery in informal settlements in Valparaíso, Chile.
criterion_notes.c2: Satisfies BOTH the plain wording of Criterion 2 and the narrow 2026-10-13 rule-type mechanism reading. Under the plain wording, the study examines water governance, privatization under Chile's 1981 Water Code, and municipal/utility service provision. Under the narrow 2026-10-13 rule-type reading, the study empirically analyzes concrete legal, administrative, and regulatory rules directly governing service access: (1) land-tenure irregularity and legal site-recognition requirements ('reconocimiento de la calidad legal del sitio ocupado') contrasted with private concessionaire ESVAL network coverage; (2) the official MINVU administrative cadastre eligibility rule requiring more than eight contiguous families in irregular tenure, which excludes 67% of informal-settlement territory (124.15 ha vs 72.72 ha) from official recognition; (3) the communal regulatory urban boundary ('límite urbano definido por el Plan Regulador Comunal') and Ley 20.038 / 'certificado de factibilidad' concession obligations governing formal service provision inside vs outside the urban limit; and (4) privatized utility ownership/concession structure versus municipal tanker delivery rules and tariffs ($10 per 6,000 L weekly potable delivery vs $0.0016/L formal private tariff).
criterion_notes.c3: Mixed-methods empirical study combining primary data (drone orthophotogrammetric surveys of 57 informal settlements in Jan–Jun 2018, semi-structured interviews with 20 residents across 4 settlement systems in Jan–Sep 2018, and in-situ planimetric mapping of water storage infrastructure) with secondary spatial/administrative datasets (2017 Census, SISS reports, ESVAL and MOP water network GIS layers, MINVU/TECHO campamento cadastres, and Ministerio de Bienes Nacionales land-tenure records).
criterion_notes.c4: Reports concrete access, exclusion, quantity, affordability/price, and reliability outcomes: 3,122 dwellings inside the Valparaíso urban boundary lack drinking water and sewerage; formal water/sewer networks terminate at 260 msnm leaving 11 informal settlement systems (260–410 msnm) in the Urban-Forest Interface Zone unserved; 9 of 11 systems rely on wells, springs, informal connections, and municipal tanker trucks; households receive an average of 24,000 L/month via tanker trucks at $10 per 6,000 L (~$0.0016/L) without sewerage or network maintenance and face irregular delivery due to weather and steep topography.
criterion_notes.c5: Population and unit of analysis (informal settlements / 24 urban-geographic settlement systems—specifically 11 systems in the ZIUF—plus dwellings and 20 interviewed residents in Valparaíso, Chile), rule-type legal/administrative exposures, service-access outcomes, and mixed-methods spatial/qualitative case-study design are all clearly identified.
criterion_notes.c6: Full text is in Spanish (with English, Portuguese, Spanish, and French abstracts). Eligible under Criterion 10 because translation from the provided Spanish full text is directly feasible and the empirical socio-legal/spatial study is substantively important to the review; translation feasibility should be logged in extraction_note during data extraction.

study_design: Mixed-methods empirical case study combining GIS spatial analysis (drone orthophotogrammetry, in-situ planimetric mapping, census, land-tenure cadastre, and utility network overlays) with 20 semi-structured resident interviews
population_and_sample: Informal settlements in Valparaíso, Chile: 57 officially catastrados campamentos (2,716 families) and uncatastrados informal housing areas forming 24 urban-geographic settlement systems (focusing on 11 systems in the Urban-Forest Interface Zone [ZIUF]), 117,196 communal dwellings in the 2017 Census, and 20 interviewed inhabitants across 4 settlement systems (Torres de Mesana, Cuesta Colorada, Violeta Parra, and Los Lancheros). Units of analysis: settlement system and household/dwelling.
exposure: Irregular land tenure status ('reconocimiento de la calidad legal del sitio ocupado'), MINVU official campamento cadastre threshold (>8 contiguous families in irregular tenure), communal urban regulatory boundary (Plan Regulador Comunal / Ley 20.038 formal utility service-area obligation and 'certificado de factibilidad'), and privatized water concession structure (1981 Water Code / ESVAL S.A.) versus municipal tanker truck delivery rules.
outcome: Formal drinking water and sewerage network coverage/exclusion (3,122 unserved dwellings inside the urban limit; absence of network above 260 msnm across 11 ZIUF settlement systems), reliance on informal connections/wells/springs and municipal water tanker trucks (9 of 11 systems), household tanker water volume (mean 24,000 L/month), tariff/price ($10 per 6,000 L weekly potable delivery vs $0.0016/L private utility rate), and delivery irregularity/lack of sewerage.
rationale: This mixed-methods spatial and qualitative study empirically examines household and settlement-level drinking water and sewerage access in informal settlements in Valparaíso, Chile. It satisfies all inclusion criteria under both the plain wording and the narrow 2026-10-13 rule-type reading of Criterion 2 by overlaying land-tenure records, the MINVU >8-family administrative cadastre threshold (which excludes 67% of informal-settlement area), the Plan Regulador Comunal urban boundary / Ley 20.038 utility service-obligation rules (showing 21 of 24 informal systems lie inside the urban boundary yet lack formal coverage above 260 msnm), and private utility ESVAL network maps, alongside primary drone surveys, planimetric mapping, and 20 resident interviews documenting municipal tanker pricing, quantities, and service reliability. Although written in Spanish (with an English abstract), full-text translation is directly feasible under Criterion 10.
